posts.author: Nox_Aeternae
posts.body:
My first instinct is to give a non-answer and say "whatever system fits your game." While I think that's the most "correct" answer, and that you should use the system that fits your goals of what you want your game to be, I will try to give a more helpful response:
I, personally, am not a big fan of AB systems and prefer a more standard turn-based system. But I'm also aware that there are a lot of people who do enjoy AB systems. For me, the most important thing to get right with an AB system is to make it snappy. Clunky hitboxes, delayed responses and sluggish movement/attacks will turn me away from a game before you can blink.
Massive amounts of the same enemy + enemies respawning immediately upon map change are also pet peeves of mine. That being said, I think there are ways to make hordes of enemies work a la Vampire Survivors but the execution needs to be impeccable for it to feel fun with enough customization/depth.
For a more standard turn-based system, I think key is to have enough depth for the players to feel smart about their decisions without bloating their UI with skills that they will use once in a blue moon.
I think you should also take into consideration your narrative + the design of the rest of your game so that the battle system doesn't feel out of place from the rest of the game.

posts.author: Big_D
posts.body:
From what you're typing it's clear you don't yet have much experience with RPG Maker yet. Don't let some shovelware on Steam fool you, this isn't an engine where you can put in minimum effort and get the results you or anybody else wants. The time you invest and the cohesion between your ideas shows in the final product.
The best thing you can do is take a stab at any ideas you have, no matter how outlandish, without the expectation that it will end up in a commercial game. If you spend 50 hours on a game that isn't coming together, it's not a waste, you'll have good ideas in there you can implement and improve upon in the future. Don't be too prideful to use plugins either - other people have already done a
lot
of work for you and the most they usually ask is a name in the credits. I have 200 hours in VX Ace from a few years back and while it never produced anything remotely good, all that experience has gone on to be immensely helpful in MV.
The most important thing is your combat system. That is where the bulk of your early work has to go. Look at games you enjoy, look at how their combat works, and see if you can come up with some facsimile of it in RPG Maker.
If you like games like Final Fantasy 7, try Active Turn Battle.
If you like games like Final Fantasy X or Labyrinth of Touhou 2, try Charge Turn Battle.
If you like games like Persona 5, End Roll or Artificial Dream in Arcadia, then stick with the default combat and see if you can put some unique spins on it.
If you like games like Mad Father and Ib, maybe try an RPG without combat. It might work better than you'd think.
Asking other people what should be at the beating heart of
your
game will never work because it should be the kind of game that speaks to
you
. If you didn't enjoy making it, it comes through in the game. Shed your expectations, let ambition take you by the wind, and maybe you'll find your calling.

posts.author: LindyGraham
posts.body:
Maybe try downshifting and opting to have a handful of completed game experiences for under your belt first, instead of immediately trying to chase dollars probably would be quite prudent. It also would provide some quality learning experience for the longterm granting efficient productivity in the future projects.
There is a Navy Seal mantra that probably should be cited as being positive advice to follow in most situations.
" Slow is smooth, smooth is fast "
Start off with something you know how to execute. Complete a short project first. Then create a slightly more complex project and repeat exponentially as you learn to improve your skill set.
Have you talked to your friends outside of the forum? They are teenagers and in your 'target audience', right? Have they played around with RM, or games that emulate the battle mechanics in a similar manner? Do they have established preferences?
* also maybe you want to disclose what plugins you already possess, if you haven't already. We don't know your financing for your project and stating what battle system plugins you already own may help narrow some suggestions and streamline your project to being worked on, rather than putting the project entirely on hold until you are able to attain 'said' battle system plugin so as to continue progress.
-but, that's just my take.
You do you.
You have agency over your choices in life.
No one is twisting any arms here.
Everyone is responsible for choices they enact even if said choice may stem from the advice of another.
Only you can choose what is personally best for yourself
-LG

posts.author: ZimXero
posts.body: I think ATB is the most popular overall.  CTB gets used a lot for turn but it does not allow interrupts and it requires a detailed plan to balance it, or speed becomes the overriding characteristic.  Tactical is something a whole lot of us want... but only if it's done well and isn't just a time sink.  Some of the hybrid systems are as good as the game is... so it depends on your game.   I recommend using ATB unless you are making a very unusual game or a long and complex game.

posts.author: Oggy
posts.body:
I am personally a fan of turn-based as long as its not over complicated. I like the ability to take my time and stratagize as I go.
The only addition to this is active wait turn-based (time bars all stop while acting). Because it lets you plan but also be reactive throughout combat. This also helps combat go a bit quicker, meaning you can add some better mechanics or larger troop sizes.
Best way to balance agility/speed I've found is make the stat static. Figure out the min max for the stat for all, like 1 - 33. Each player actor gets a number between 10 and 17. Then limit the use of the stat. Meaning you don't gain it by leveling and only a few items may increase it. In fact of you characters can use multiple weapon types this is a great place to use decreases for more  powerful weapon types (two handers for instance.

Publishing a commercial game isn't the challenge. You can upload anything on Itch and slap a pricetag on it. You now have a commercial game.
The challenge is making it appealing enough to a market for them to want to buy it, and making those people aware your product exists.
So you need to research what (low budget indie) games do "serious teen gamers" currently buy, and at what price point, so you know what they expect in the games they buy.

To answer the question originally posed here, I personally like to have a couple battle systems for long games, for short games I like ABS the most.  For example, my first game had ABS and Tower Defense.  I used the ABS for majority of the game but switched to Tower Defense just for specific battles when you were defending a city.  This gave it a little change that made a big difference. Wasn't always the same battle look.  This was a game you couldn't beat in less than 70 hours.  For a short game don't add 2 battle systems, it's not worth it.  Only reason 2 worked for that one was the game length.
A little side note, Echo607 on Youtube, said something that really stuck with me when making my games.  "Make the game you want to play".  Just a very good piece of advice.  If you're going commercial or not, I would just follow her advice on that.

posts.author: PlayGG_Doctor
posts.body:
The way I see it, if you are trying to hook as many people as possible and sell as many copies as possible in the ultra-saturated indie RPG market, you need to do one of two things:
1)
Have a hook that no other game has
(ideally, or realistically, that very few other games have used) - For example, remember when Undertale came out and had two hooks: 1) All fights can be won without violence and 2) the battles themselves would be a combination of bullet hell dodging and timed button presses. Copycats like Everhood came out and expanded on the "musical dodging" combat and also did quite well. So, it doesn't have to be entirely unique, but it shouldn't be something that's been done a million times.
2)
Do something that's been done, but make it complex and interesting -
If your target audience is hardcore RPG fans, then take a page out of Persona and Shin Megami Tensei's book and make the turn based battles HARD, requiring both a lot of preparation before combat as well as an understanding of how to exploit enemy weaknesses to even have a chance. No one wants to pay for a game that just has regular turn based combat where you mash A to attack during every battle. Its just been done to death. And giving every character 100 available equipment options and 100 spells also doesnt move the needle by itself because players will just pick whatever equipment has the highest stats and spam whatever abilities seem most efficient at ending combat. You will need to force players to consider their choices whether it be by making resources very limited, or by making enemies very strong and requiring the player to make careful, tactical choices to win.
This is the best advice I can give short of just telling specifically and exactly what type of combat system to use, and that really is something you need to decide for yourself. Best of luck, dev!
